Signs and symptoms include a vaginal mass, vaginal pressure, perinea! discomfort, and urinary or fecal retention or incontinence. Management may include the insertion of a vaginal pessary, which is a mechanical device that provides pelvic support, along with pelvic floor exercises. If noninvasive therapies fail, surgical treatment with reconstruction, fixation, uterine suspension, or hysterectomy can be considered.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice A) has no role in diagnosing pelvic support defects. Evaluation of pelvic support defects is clinical with a speculum examination, and may also include urinalysis, cystoscopy, or evaluation of post-void residual volume. Endometrial biopsy (Choice B) is used in the evaluation for abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in women over 45 years of age or in postmenopausal women for the investigation of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Cervical amputation (Choice D) and vaginal hysterectomy (Choice E) may be used in the treatment of pelvic support defects, however, surgical management of uterine prolapse is typically considered later, after attempting noninvasive management. These techniques may be difficult to ethically justify in an elderly person with dementia depending on the patient's goals of care and relative safety for surgery. Educational Objective: Pelvic support defects causing urogenital prolapse are typically to the result of the loss of connective tissue and muscular support of the uterus, paravaginal tissue, bladder wall, urethra, or distal rectum. Management may include the insertion of a vaginal pessary, which is a mechanical device that improves pelvic support, along with pelvic floor exercises. If noninvasive therapies fail, surgical treatment with reconstruction, fixation, uterine suspension, or hysterectomy can be considered.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports that she has felt little movement of the fetus during the past 18 hours. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated . She weighed 59 kg (130 lb) prior to her pregnancy ; BMI was 22 kg/m 2• She has had a 9.5-kg (28-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy . Her pulse is 72/min , and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. The fundal height is 29 cm. No fetal heart tones are heard on Doppler. On pelvic examination , the cervix is closed and not effaced . Urine dipstick shows no glucose or protein. Ultrasonography confirms the absence of fetal cardiac activity in an otherwise normal-appearing male fetus . The patient and her husband choose to return home to await spontaneous labor. Four weeks later, the patient comes to the physician because of an episode of light vaginal bleeding but no contractions . External electronic monitoring shows mild irregular contractions every 20 to 30 minutes . The cervix is closed and not effaced , and the presenting part is soft and at -2 station . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Hematocrit Platelet count Plasma fibrinogen 11 g/dL 32% 90,000/mm 3 250 mg/dL (N=20-400) Stillbirth refers to fetal demise after 20 weeks' gestation and can occur before or during delivery. Antepartum intrauterine fetal demise commonly presents as in this patient, with decreased fetal movement and lack of fetal heart tones on examination. Ultrasonography confirms the intrauterine fetal demise. In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly because of chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease, whereas it is more commonly caused by maternal infection, preeclampsia, or obstructed labor in low-income countries. Delivery for antepartum intrauterine fetal demise is based on the mother's wishes, with immediate induction or delayed natural delivery; both options in the absence of any complicating medical issues. Labor typically begins 1 to 2 weeks after fetal demise. Coagulation abnormalities can occur with delayed delivery because of the release of tissue factor {thromboplastin) from the placenta. This can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation {DIC), which presents with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of partial thromboplastin and prothrombin time, increased d-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration. Given this patient's early mild contractions, closed cervix, prolonged retention of a nonviable fetus, and risk for the development of coagulation abnormalities, induction of labor is the most appropriate next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma {Choice B) is typically performed in patients with coagulation abnormalities that put them at increased risk for bleeding, such as supratherapeutic international normalized ratio {INR) or DIC. As this patient has yet to develop coagulation abnormalities, treatment with fresh frozen plasma is inappropriate. Transfusion of platelets {Choice C) is indicated when a patient's platelets fall below 10,000/mm 3 or below 50,000/mm 3 when they are actively bleeding or require a surgical intervention or invasive procedure. This patient's platelets are 90,000/mm 3, making a platelet transfusion inappropriate at this time. Cesarean delivery {Choice D) can be used to deliver fetuses in the setting of arrest of labor, cephalopelvic disproportion, and placenta or vasa previa but is not typically required in intrauterine fetal demise. Following fetal death, there is a collapse and maceration of the fetal body, which allows most fetuses to undergo successful vaginal delivery. Dilation and curettage {Choice E) can be used in elective abortion or to remove remaining fetal tissue in a missed or incomplete spontaneous abortion. However, as this fetal demise occurred at 32 weeks, the fetus is likely too large to be removed with dilation and curettage. Educational Objective: Stillbirth refers to the demise of a fetus after 20 weeks' gestation and can occur before or during delivery. For antepartum intrauterine fetal demise, immediate induction or delayed natural labor are both options, but prolonged retention of a nonviable fetus increases the risk for developing DIC in the mother because of the release of thromboplastin from the placenta.

questionStem: A 25-year-old primigravid woman is in labor at 24 weeks' gestation . Treatment with a tocolytic agent is ineffective . She has used crack cocaine during the pregnancy . Cocaine most likely altered her uterine contractility by which of the following mechanisms?
correctExplanation: Crack cocaine is a sympathomimetic that increases sympathetic tone through the inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. This results in an increased synaptic norepinephrine concentration and consequent increased adrenergic receptor activation. This increased sympathetic tone results in the activation of aradrenergic receptors on the uterine myometrial smooth muscle myocytes, leading to increased contraction. This abnormally increased, unregulated contraction of uterine smooth muscle can result in the onset of preterm labor. Tocolytic therapy with common agents such as terbutaline (~-mimetic), magnesium sulfate, prostaglandin inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers are often ineffective at reducing uterine contractions, as they do not directly inhibit the sympathetic activation of the uterine myocytes, which is increased in the setting of cocaine use. Cocaine use in pregnancy can also cause uteroplacental insufficiency with low birth weight or intrauterine growth restriction, miscarriage, and abruptio placentae as a result of sympathetic stimulation and resultant vasoconstriction.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreasing catecholamines (Choice A) would cause relaxation of the uterine smooth muscle. However, cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine in the synapse, increasing sympathetic tone and uterine contractility. Decreasing parasympathetic tone (Choice B) may lead to smooth muscle contraction because of a relative increase in sympathetic tone compared to parasympathetic tone, but this is not the mechanism of action of crack cocaine. Increasing norepinephrine reuptake (Choice D) would decrease the amount of norepinephrine available for adrenergic receptor stimulation, which would cause a relative decrease in sympathetic stimulation and a decrease in smooth muscle contraction. Cocaine, on the contrary, inhibits norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. Increasing parasympathetic tone (Choice E) would lead to uterine smooth muscle relaxation, rather than contraction, as seen in this patient. This is not the mechanism of crack cocaine. Educational Objective: Crack cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic because of the inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. In pregnancy, this increased sympathetic tone increases the risk for abnormal uterine smooth muscle contractions and potential preterm labor. Cocaine is also associated with an increased risk for uteroplacental insufficiency, miscarriage, low birth weight, and abruptio placentae.

questionStem: Two days after spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy newborn at term, a previously healthy 37-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, has left-sided pleuritic chest pain and progressive shortness of breath . Her pulse is 94/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 96/55 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. Examination of the extremities shows mild edema and no tenderness . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.1 g/dl , and leukocyte count is 15,500/mm 3• Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows : Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.C: Fetal squamous cells in the pulmonary veins

correctExplanation: 7.45 21 mm Hg 85 mm Hg Pulmonary embolism classically presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and clear breath sounds, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state (eg, pregnancy). Small pulmonary emboli may present only as pain or subjective shortness of breath and may be asymptomatic with normal vital signs. By contrast, large emboli with pulmonary infarctions generally cause more severe symptoms, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, and potentially hypotension if significant enough to obstruct cardiac output. The resultant tachypnea is demonstrated on arterial blood gas analysis as an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation leading to diminished arterial carbon dioxide, and as hypoxemia because of the ventilated but not perfused affected lung segments. Pelvic venous congestion is a common source of deep venous thrombosis in pregnancy. Large pulmonary emboli may be seen on chest x-ray by secondary signs, such as wedge-shaped areas of infarction or via the Westermark sign of unilateral oligemia, though the standard of diagnosis is CT pulmonary angiography. In pregnancy, a ventilation-perfusion scan may be preferred as this technique is safer for the fetus (less radiation exposure). The ECG in a pulmonary embolus often shows sinus tachycardia, and if there is right heart strain can exhibit right axis deviation, S wave in lead I, Q wave in lead 111, and inverted T wave in lead Ill ('S1Q3T3'). Treatment depends on the risk for bleeding to the patient but includes systemic anticoagulation or surgical thrombectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Bronchial smooth muscle contractions (Choice A) describe the pathophysiology of asthma and reactive airway disease. Obstruction to airflow through constricted small airways presents with shortness of breath and wheezing, hyperventilation or hypoventilation if severe, and generally with vital signs reflecting tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Examination shows wheezing and respiratory distress. This patient's breath sounds are clear, making this a less likely diagnosis. Exudates in the alveoli (Choice B) describes pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome. Pneumonia presents with cough, pleuritic chest pain, fever, and chills, and often follows an upper respiratory infection or aspiration event. Vital signs may be normal or show signs of sepsis (tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia). Auscultation generally discloses focal or diffuse rhonchi and egophony; examination may show dullness to percussion. Fetal squamous cells in the pulmonary veins (Choice C) describe an amniotic fluid embolism, a rare and life-threatening complication that occurs when amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation. It classically presents with acute, severe shortness of breath, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy during labor. It would be less likely to occur 2 days following delivery. Mucus trapping in the bronchioles (Choice D) describes the pathophysiology of acute or chronic bronchitis, or cystic fibrosis. These entities present with cough productive of sputum, and rhonchorous breath sounds. Educational Objective: Pulmonary embolism classically presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and clear breath sounds, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state (eg, pregnancy). The resultant tachypnea is demonstrated on arterial blood gas analysis as an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation and as hypoxemia because of the ventilated but not perfused affected lung segments.

questionStem: A 4508-g (9-lb 15-oz) male newborn is delivered at 41 weeks' gestation to a 37-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1. Pregnancy and labor were complicated by mild preeclampsia treated with an infusion of magnesium sulfate during labor. Electronic fetal monitoring showed a normal fetal heart rate and pattern . A pudenda! block with 1 % lidocaine was given for analgesia . The newborn was delivered with forceps after the fetal heart rate decreased to 80/min in the second stage of labor. The shoulders were firmly impacted , and the newborn was delivered after 3 minutes using special maneuvers . Apgar scores are 3 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . Examination shows no motion of the right side of the face , even when the child cries . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Assisted vaginal delivery is indicated for a prolonged second stage of labor or in the setting of fetal distress, as seen in this patient with fetal bradycardia. It can be completed using vacuum-assisted devices or metal forceps. Successful assisted vaginal delivery requires a dilated and effaced cervix with ruptured membranes and an engaged occiput. Vacuum-assisted delivery is typically chosen when extraction is expected to be easy, although it is relatively contraindicated in fetuses with a gestational age less than 34 weeks. Forceps are chosen when the extraction is expected to be more difficult and require fetal head rotation. Vacuum­ assisted devices can cause scalp lacerations, cephalohematoma, brachia! plexus injury caused by shoulder dystocia, retinal hemorrhage, and intracranial hemorrhage. Forceps-assisted deliveries carry the risk for laceration, intracranial hemorrhage, facial nerve injury, skull fracture, and ocular injury. Mothers can also suffer from lacerations, urinary tract injury, and anal sphincter injury. Facial nerve injury from forceps delivery will present in the neonate with unilateral facial paralysis, as seen in this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Brachia! plexus injury (Choice A) most commonly presents with Erb-Duchenne palsy following birth because of traction placed on the upper brachia! plexus trunks during delivery. Erb-Duchenne palsy commonly causes adduction of the shoulder with internal rotation of the arm, extension of the elbow, pronation of the forearm, and flexion of the fingers and wrists. It does not cause facial muscle paralysis. Cerebral palsy (Choice B) is a neuromuscular disorder that is commonly caused by hypoxia during delivery, although it is also associated with congenital abnormalities, preterm birth, perinatal stroke, maternal smoking, and intrauterine growth restriction. It typically presents with dyskinesia, involuntary movements, ataxia, and spasticity. However, the diagnosis is not often clinically apparent at birth. lntracranial hemorrhage (Choice D) is an unusual complication of vaginal delivery in a term infant. It could potentially present with unilateral facial paralysis but would likely occur in association with contralateral extremity hemiparesis, which is not seen in this patient. Lidocaine toxicity (Choice E) presents with altered mental status, slurred speech, nystagmus, and seizures. It would not be expected to cause facial paralysis in the newborn following a pudenda! nerve block. Magnesium toxicity (Choice F) can occur following intravenous magnesium therapy and presents in the mother with loss of deep tendon reflexes, decreased respirations, and oliguria, as well as changes on electrocardiography. It can lead to fetal bradycardia and a decrease in fetal heart rate variability but would not cause facial muscle paralysis. Educational Objective: Assisted vaginal delivery with vacuum devices or forceps is indicated for a prolonged second stage of labor or in the setting of fetal distress. Both can cause scalp lacerations, intracranial hemorrhage, and ocular injury. Vacuum-assisted delivery carries the additional risk for brachia! plexus injury, and forceps-assisted delivery can increase the risk for facial nerve injury or skull fracture.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman with leiomyomata uteri comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . She has not had vaginal bleeding , pelvic pain, or loss of urine. Examination shows no abnormalities except for a uterus consistent in size with a 15-week gestation . Her hematocrit is 41 %. Pelvic ultrasonography confirms leiomyomata uteri. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: In this patient with asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri (also known as uterine fibroids), the most appropriate management is observation only. Leiomyomata uteri are common benign tumors of the uterine smooth muscle. In many patients, leiomyomata uteri are asymptomatic, though in other patients, leiomyomata uteri can lead to abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, and/or reproductive dysfunction. Physical examination may demonstrate an enlarged, lobulated uterus, and the presence of leiomyomata uteri can be confirmed with ultrasonography. Since leiomyomata uteri are benign and may regress over time or with menopause, asymptomatic lesions should be managed expectantly. For symptomatic leiomyomata uteri, hysteroscopic or abdominal myomectomy is often the first-line treatment. In patients who do not desire pregnancy, alternative treatments include oral contraceptive therapy, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist therapy, and hysterectomy (oral contraceptive and GnRH agonist therapy can lead to rebound symptoms when discontinued to allow for conception).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous pyelography (Choice B) is utilized to visualize the urinary tract, not the uterus. In intravenous pyelography, iodine contrast dye is injected, and imaging is obtained when the contrast fills the lumen of the urinary tract to disclose tract pathology, such as nephrolithiasis, tumors, and strictures. Myomectomy (Choice E) is a first-line treatment option for symptomatic uterine fibroids, which involves the surgical removal of one or multiple specific leiomyomata uteri. GnRH agonist therapy (Choice C), oral contraceptive therapy (Choice D), and hysterectomy are also treatment considerations for symptomatic leiomyomata uteri in patients who do not desire to preserve fertility. However, any of these options should only be considered for patients with symptomatic leiomyomata uteri, not for this patient without symptoms. Educational Objective: Leiomyomata uteri are common benign tumors of the smooth muscle. Asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri are managed expectantly with observation, while leiomyomata uteri that cause symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, or reproductive dysfunction can be managed with myomectomy (leiomyomata uteri removal), oral contraceptive therapy, GnRH therapy agonists, or hysterectomy.

questionStem: A 19-year-old woman comes to student health services because of a 5-day history of an ulcer on the inner side of the right vulva . Six weeks ago, she was diagnosed with herpes simplex virus 2 involving the left side of the vulva . At that time, testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae was negative . HIV antibody testing and rapid plasma reagin were also negative . She has completed a 10-day course of valacyclovir therapy. She has not been sexually active since her last examination . Today, she reports that her herpes sores are gone. Pelvic examination shows a 1 x 2.5-cm nontender ulcer with slightly raised edges and a shallow base on the perineum . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.C: Repeat testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae

correctExplanation: A variety of sexually transmitted infections may cause formation of a nontender genital ulcer. These include lymphogranuloma venereum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L 1, L2, and L3, syphilitic chancre caused by Treponema pallidum, and granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiel/a granulomatis. In contrast, genital herpes and chancroid, caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and Haemophilus ducreyi, respectively, are both characterized by painful genital ulcers. The organisms causing painful ulcers can be distinguished clinically based on the ulcer appearance. For example, the ulcer of chancroid is exudative and accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. The ulcer of granuloma inguinale (also called donovanosis) is beefy red, friable, and often induces additional ulcers on oppositional skin. The chancre of primary syphilis is shallow with a clean base. Thus, the ulcer described in this case fits best with the ulcer of primary syphilis and testing for this infection should be pursued. Untreated syphilis demonstrates multiple stages with varying symptoms, including primary with a painless chancre as described, secondary with fever, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, and tertiary with tabes dorsalis, aortitis, and gummas. Serologic testing for syphilis is first performed with a nontreponemal test, such as a venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test or rapid plasma reagin (RPR). During the early phases of primary syphilis, VDRL and RPR may be negative. Given the patient's supporting clinical evidence for primary syphilis, the RPR should be repeated. These tests are typically performed as a screening test and, if positive, should be followed up with a treponemal test, such as the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. HIV infection may be transmitted as a coinfection along with syphilis. In fact, infection with one may increase the likelihood of transmission of the second. Repeat HIV test (Choice A) may be warranted in the future of this patient but is not necessary at this time for diagnostic purposes, as the painless ulcer described is more likely because of syphilis than an HIV infection. Repeat testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice C) is unnecessary at this time. Without repeat sexual activity since the time of the first tests, it is unlikely that these would have become positive. While the L 1, L2, and L3 subtypes of Chlamydia trachomatis cause lymphogranuloma venereum, the patient's presentation is more consistent with a primary syphilitic chancre. The ulcer of lymphogranuloma venereum is exudative and accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. Viral culture of the ulcer (Choice D) would be the diagnostic test of choice for vesicular and ulcerative lesions caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). Genital herpes infections present with painful vesicles and erosions with associated lymphadenopathy. HSV-2 followed by HSV-1 are the most common viral culprits. Excision of the ulcer (Choice E) would not be appropriate in the case of an infectious ulcer as it would not treat the underlying infection. A vulvar ulcer with a neoplastic origin would be treated surgically. Educational Objective: Nontender genital ulcers may be caused by Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L 1, L2, and L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum), Treponema pallidum (primary syphilitic chancre), and Klebsiel/a granulomatis (granuloma inguinale). In contrast, HSV (genital herpes) and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) both cause painful genital ulcers.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has no history of operative procedures , and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . She has a 3-year history of hypothyroidism well controlled with levothyroxine . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. She weighed 77 kg (169 lb) prior to her pregnancy ; BMI was 29 kg/m 2• She has had a 14-kg (31-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy . Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Fundal height is 30 cm. Ultrasonography shows moderate polyhydramnios . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings ?
correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios refers to excessive concentrations of amniotic fluid volume and an associated increased uterine size relative to gestational age. It is associated with an increased risk for fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. It should be suspected when the uterine size and fundal height are larger than expected for gestational age. Polyhydramnios can be diagnosed on ultrasonography examination through measuring the amniotic fluid index (AFI). An AFI greater than 24 cm indicates an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with a variety of disorders, including maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B 19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities such as duodenal atresia or anencephaly. Fetal anomalies are the most common cause of polyhydramnios but are typically apparent on ultrasonography. Antenatal testing, such as fetal ultrasonography with biophysical profile, should be performed to evaluate for underlying fetal anomalies along with an amniocentesis to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities. The frequency of antenatal testing depends on the severity of the polyhydramnios. Given the patient's history of an uncomplicated pregnancy until this point, the most likely cause of this patient's polyhydramnios is undiagnosed maternal diabetes mellitus.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Excessive maternal hydration {Choice A) may lead to peripheral edema and hypervolemic hyponatremia but would be unlikely to alter the amount of amniotic fluid. Fetal aneuploidy {Choice B) can present with polyhydramnios but would be expected to also have apparent congenital abnormalities on ultrasonography. For example, when combined with intrauterine growth restriction, polyhydramnios is commonly as a result oftrisomy 18, which would present with rounded feet, cystic hygroma, neural tube defects, facial defects, omphalocele, and septal or valvular cardiac disease. Fetal myotonic dystrophy {Choice C) presents with hypotonia, joint contractures, respiratory muscle weakness, and bilateral facial paralysis. Polyhydramnios is common; however, inheritance is autosomal dominant, and thus the disorder would be unlikely in this patient with no family history of myotonic dystrophy. Fetal renal agenesis {Choice D) would cause oligohydramnios because of the absence of urine production, not polyhydramnios as seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios can be caused by maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (eg, duodenal atresia, anencephaly, esophageal atresia).

questionStem: A previously healthy 19-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 0, aborta 1, comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of severe pelvic pain and a pus-like vaginal discharge . Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. She has had two sexual partners during the past month and uses an oral contraceptive . Her temperature is 38.5°C (101 .3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows tenderness to palpation of the lower quadrants with no guarding or rebound . Speculum examination shows irritated vaginal and cervical mucosa with copious purulent discharge coming from the cervical os. Bimanual examination shows cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness . Rectovaginal examination shows a fluctuant mass in the cul-de-sac . In addition to testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis , which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis can both cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Vaginitis typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PID can become complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess or intraabdominal abscess, presenting with focal tenderness and a fluctuant mass. Treatment of PID involves antibiotics such as cephalosporins and tetracyclines. Risk factors for PID and other sexually transmitted infections include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and not using barrier contraception such as condoms. Patients diagnosed with PID should be tested for other common sexually transmitted infections as well, such as HIV and syphilis. Compromised mucosal barriers in the setting of genital infections present an entry point for HIV, for which this patient should also be tested.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A Pap smear (Choice A) is a part of routine health screening in women to evaluate for the presence of cervical dysplasia commonly caused by the human papillomavirus. Screening Pap smears are recommended every 3 years in women aged 21 to 29 years and every 5 years in conjunction with HPV co-testing (every 3 years if co-testing is not performed) in women aged 30 to 65 years. Pap smears are not performed for the diagnosis of sexually transmitted infections. Herpes simplex virus test (Choice B) is appropriate if genital herpes is suspected, which is characterized by painful vesicles in the genital area (eg, vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum) and may be associated with dysuria. Diagnosis of herpes can be clinical given the classic appearance of the infection, or via viral culture of any vesicles. Routine testing is less meaningful and not frequently performed, as many patients have positive serologic studies for herpes but no evidence of active or treatable infection. Human papillomavirus (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical/vulvar and penile/anal carcinoma, as well as condyloma acuminata. Testing for human papillomavirus can be done in conjunction with Pap smear cytology but is not a part of routine diagnosis for active sexually transmitted infections. Hysterosalpingography (Choice E) is performed in the evaluation of infertility to evaluate the patency of the fallopian tubes, detect developmental abnormalities such as unicornuate or septate uterus, and evaluate for the presence of polyps, submucosal myomas, or intrauterine adhesions. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis can both cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and PID, which is characterized by mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and fever. Risk factors for PID and other sexually transmitted infections include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and not using barrier contraception. Therefore, patients diagnosed with PID should be tested for other common sexually transmitted infections, such as HIV and syphilis.

questionStem: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of vague abdominal discomfort for 3 days. She has never had a menstrual period . Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows a right adnexal mass. Ultrasonography shows an 8-cm complex mass in the right adnexa with echogenicity . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Mature cystic teratomas are benign tumors of the ovary. They are the most common ovarian germ-cell tumor, and typically occur in women between the ages of 10 and 30 years old. They contain tissue derived from all three germ cell layers and, as a result, contain differentiated structures such as hair, bone, or teeth. Patients often present with abdominal or pelvic pain because of the size of the teratoma, rapid enlargement, or associated ovarian torsion. Physical examination typically demonstrates a unilateral (or bilateral) adnexal mass on pelvic examination, which may be tender. Definitive evaluation includes pelvic ultrasonography, which will demonstrate a complex cystic adnexal mass with internal echoes (hair, teeth). Occasionally, mature cystic teratomas can present with chemical peritonitis as a result of rupture, and a small percentage become malignant. The treatment for symptomatic teratomas is surgical resection.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Appendiceal abscess (Choice A) may occur as a complication of appendicitis, which presents with abdominal pain that begins in the periumbilical region and then migrates to the right lower quadrant, with associated fever, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Right lower quadrant tenderness and leukocytosis are also commonly present. Abscess formation often occurs in delayed presentation secondary to perforation of the appendix. Epithelial ovarian carcinoma (Choice B) typically presents late in stage with associated pelvic or abdominal pain and bloating and an adnexal mass on physical examination. It more commonly occurs in postmenopausal women and is associated with an increased cancer antigen 125 concentration. Functional ovarian cyst (Choice C) is a simple cystic structure of the ovary that occurs during the process of follicle development when an egg is not appropriately released from a follicle during ovulation. Patients may be asymptomatic but can present with abdominal or pelvic pain if the cyst is large. Potential complications include ovarian torsion. Follicular cysts are usually simple and do not typically present with internal echoes on ultrasonography. Hydatidiform mole (Choice D) is a form of gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by noninvasive diffuse swelling of chorionic tissue as caused by the abnormal fertilization of an ovum. It is unlikely in this patient who has yet to ovulate and would be more commonly associated with an enlarged uterus rather than an adnexal mass. Educational Objective: Mature cystic teratomas are benign tumors of the ovary derived from all three germ cell layers, and thus commonly contain mature structures such as teeth, hair, and bone. Definitive evaluation includes pelvic ultrasonography, which will demonstrate a complex cystic adnexal mass with internal echoes.

questionStem: Seven days after undergoing an abdominal hysterectomy , a 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she has not voided since discharge 36 hours ago. She describes no unusual pain since discharge . Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min , and blood pressure is 112/7 4 mm Hg. Examination shows a clean incision and a soft symmetric mass that extends 25 cm above the symphysis . Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine 12.8 g/dL 7800/mm 3 30 mg/dL 3 mg/dL Serum electrolyte concentrations are within normal limits . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings ?
correctExplanation: Postoperative urinary retention is a common medical complication of surgery. The patient will typically present with anuria or oliguria, abdominal pain, difficulty initiating or maintaining a urine stream, and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying, as well as a palpable suprapubic mass as seen in this patient. Laboratory evaluation will show an increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine concentrations, although the ratio will typically be less than 20. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, which will show a distended bladder. Treatment requires bladder catheterization to allow for appropriate emptying of the urinary bladder. Risk factors include an age greater than 50 years, preexisting urinary retention, surgery length greater than 2 hours, regional anesthesia, anticholinergic medications, and intravenous fluid resuscitation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Pelvic hematoma (Choice A) could present with a suprapubic mass after pelvic surgery, as well as urinary retention if the hematoma was large enough to compress the ureters or urethra. However, a hematoma that large would likely be associated with a decreased hemoglobin concentration, making this an unlikely cause of the patient's anuria. Prerenal azotemia (Choice B) refers to an acute kidney injury secondary to decreased renal blood flow, which results in a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR), commonly in the setting of hypovolemia, hypotension, or renal hypoperfusion. This typically presents with a fractional excretion of sodium < 1 % (increased angiotensin and aldosterone production) and a BUN to creatinine ratio> 20, as decreased tubular flow results in the reabsorption of urea but not creatinine. A retroperitoneal urinoma (Choice C) is typically caused by trauma to the kidney, which results in extravasation of urine into the perirenal fat and retroperitoneum. It presents with flank pain and is evident on ultrasonography and CT scans. It does not present with a suprapubic mass. Ureteral transection (Choice D) is a risk during hysterectomy, as the ureters travel near the uterine arteries bilaterally. It can also present with abdominal pain secondary to a urinoma or ascites as caused by the leakage of urine into the abdominal cavity, as well as nausea, vomiting, and fever. Complications include abscess formation and sepsis. It would be unlikely to present with increased creatinine or a suprapubic mass. Educational Objective: Postoperative urinary retention is a common complication of surgery. It presents with anuria or oliguria, a suprapubic mass on physical examination , and a potential acute kidney injury. Ultrasonography is diagnostic, and treatment requires bladder catheterization.

questionStem: A married 37-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 17 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She is Rh-negative , and an antibody screening at 12 weeks' gestation was negative . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Amniocentesis is done , and the amniotic fluid is grossly bloody. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Serial measurement of fetal antibody titers
choices.B: Serial measurement of maternal antibody titers
choices.C: Maternal intramuscular administration of pooled immune globulin now
choices.D: Maternal intramuscular administration of Rho(Q) immune globulin now
choices.E: Maternal intramuscular administration of Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation and after delivery

correctExplanation: F) Maternal intravenous administration of corticosteroids now G) Fetal transfusion of Rh-negative blood now H) Fetal transfusion of Rh-positive blood now I) Amniocentesis for determination of /1 OD 450 in the late second or early third trimester J) No action Rh-negative mothers are at a high risk for developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies if exposed to blood from a Rh-positive fetus. While this commonly occurs at delivery, it can also occur prior to delivery with procedures such as amniocentesis, as seen in this patient. If Rh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother's immune system will form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen. This can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the fetus (erythroblastosis fetalis) as the mother's antibodies may cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of the fetus's red blood cells (RBCs). Rh0(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh(D) antigen. It is commonly given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks of gestation, after delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, after any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and after any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management in this patient would be to provide Rho(D) immune globulin now, in order to prevent her from developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Serial measurements of fetal antibody titers (Choice A) would not determine whether the mother has developed anti-Rh(D) antibodies in response to the amniocentesis. Frequent blood assessments of the fetus also come with associated risks, such as further bleeding, infection, and fetal death. Serial measurements of maternal antibody titers (Choice B) would allow the practitioner to determine whether she has developed anti-Rh(D) antibodies in response to the amniocentesis. However, the better option in this case would be to prevent antibody formation in the first place. Maternal intramuscular administration of pooled immune globulin now (Choice C) and maternal intravenous administration of corticosteroids (Choice F) would not provide protection against the development of anti-Rh(D) antibodies, for which this mother is at risk. Antibodies directed against Rh-positive cells would provide more adequate protection. Maternal intramuscular administration of Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation and after delivery (Choice E) would also be appropriate in this Rh-negative patient. However, without receiving Rho(D) immune globulin now, she would be at risk for developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies because of her exposure to fetal blood during the amniocentesis. Fetal transfusion of Rh-negative blood (Choice G) or Rh-positive blood (Choice H) is inappropriate, as it is not currently indicated and the fetal blood type is unknown, thus transfusion could lead to hemolytic anemia as a result of incompatible blood types. It is more appropriate to prevent the development of anti-Rh(D) antibodies and the subsequent fetal hemolytic anemia than to prophylactically treat the anemia. Amniocentesis for determination of /1 OD 450 in the late second or early third trimester (Choice I) can accurately diagnose severe fetal hemolytic anemia in the setting of Rh(D) alloimmunization, because of the presence of increased bilirubin in the amniotic fluid. However, the risk for alloimmunization can be reduced by administering Rho(D) immune globulin now. No action (Choice J) is inappropriate, as exposure to fetal blood can cause Rh(D) alloimmunization in a Rh-negative mother, which can in turn cause erythroblastosis fetalis and fetal death. It can be prevented with the administration of Rho(D) immune globulin now. Educational Objective: Rh-negative mothers are at a high risk for Rh(D) alloimmunization when exposed to Rh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation. Alloimmunization can be prevented by the administration of Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks of gestation, after delivery of an Rh(D)-positive fetus, after any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and after any episodes of fetomaternal hemorrhage.

questionStem: An obese 35-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, with type 2 diabetes mellitus has a cesarean delivery because of fetal macrosomia . Forty-eight hours later, there is profuse serosanguineous drainage from the midline skin incision . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Postoperative complications following an abdominal incision include bleeding, infection, dehiscence, hematoma formation, and seroma formation, as well as damage to nearby structures. Dehiscence occurs when the fascial tension is greater than the sutures holding the two layers of fascia together, which leads to disruption of the connection and leakage of the contents below the suture line. In abdominal incisions, dehiscence can occur at the fascial plane while the skin sutures remain intact. It typically presents, as in this patient, with prominent serosanguinous drainage, along with a possible bulge at the surgical site. Ultrasonography and CT scans can be used to further delineate the diagnosis if there is difficulty in assessing the surgical site with physical examination. Treatment involves operative exploration of the wound site to repair the fascial dehiscence, as this places the patient at an increased risk for poor wound healing, wound infection, and evisceration, which is a surgical emergency. Risk factors include elderly age, male gender, wound infection, obesity, malignancy, hypoalbuminemia, and chronic glucocorticoid use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Evisceration (Choice B) typically occurs following a complete fascial dehiscence of an abdominal incision, in which the internal abdominopelvic organs (eg, bowel) are expelled from the surgical site and are visible on examination. It is a surgical emergency and requires emergent operative management to close the wound. Hematoma (Choice C) typically presents with induration, pain, and bloody drainage of the wound. It can be managed expectantly or drained depending on size. It would be unlikely to present with simple serosanguinous drainage. Wound infection (Choice D) is a common complication of surgery, and presents with erythema, warmth, tenderness, and induration with purulent wound drainage. It typically requires antibiotic treatment and potentially surgical debridement or irrigation depending on the severity and extent of infection. As this patient's wound is draining serosanguinous, rather than purulent fluid, it is less likely a result of a wound infection. Vesicocutaneous fistula (Choice E) refers to a fistulous tract created between the bladder and outside surface of the body through the skin. It would present with the drainage of urine at the wound site, rather than serosanguinous discharge. While possible, this is a relatively unlikely complication of a cesarean delivery. Educational Objective: Postoperative wound dehiscence typically presents with serosanguinous drainage at the surgical wound site and increases the risk for evisceration, which is a surgical emergency. It requires operative management for wound closure.

questionStem: A 22-year-old college student comes to student health services because of vulvar irritation for 14 days . She is sexually active and has had three partners since the age of 15 years ; she uses an oral contraceptive . Examination shows multiple 5- to 10-mm soft pink papillary lesions with areas of pigmentation on the labia minora and posterior fourchette . The vagina and cervix appear normal , and there is no vaginal discharge . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
correctExplanation: Soft, pink, papillary lesions on the external genitalia are consistent with condyloma acuminata, genital warts associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) that can appear on the penis, vagina, vulva, or anal canal. Multiple sexual partners and the failure to use condoms during sexual intercourse are risk factors for their development. The most implicated strains of HPV are 6 and 11, which both have low oncogenic potential. High risk HPV strains include 16, 18, 31, and 33, which may also be present and indicate a higher risk for progression to cervical dysplasia and malignancy. Diagnosis is made with examination or biopsy if necessary, which will show papillomatous lesions with virally infected cells called koilocytes in the epidermis. The goal of treatment of condyloma acuminata is to destroy the affected cells, but many methods can be used to achieve this. Topical formulations of podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid, fluorouracil, or liquid nitrogen are potential agents. Immune therapy is also used, primarily with topical imiquimod, which stimulates the local innate immune system through toll-like receptors. Activation of the local immune system then leads to recognition of viral particles and an adaptive response is mounted.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acyclovir therapy (Choice A) is the first-line treatment of herpes simplex virus (HSV) genital infection. Genital herpes is most caused by HSV-2 and is characterized by painful vesicles in the genital area (eg, vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum). Infection typically begins with the formation of vesicles, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border. Azithromycin (Choice B) is an antibiotic treatment for Chlamydia trachomatis, a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Interferon therapy (Choice C) is a treatment used for severe condyloma acuminata. It is administered directly into the lesion and is expensive. It is usually reserved for refractory disease, so is not yet indicated in this patient. Zidovudine (AZT) therapy (Choice E) is a component of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) used to treat HIV infection. HIV infection can initially be asymptomatic, or it can present as an acute retroviral syndrome in the weeks following inoculation. HIV and HPV often infect the same individual. In this case, the condyloma acuminata may become florid and difficult to treat. While HIV testing may be prudent in this patient given her sexual history, there are no signs of current HIV infection and thus no need for HAART at this time. Radiation therapy (Choice F) is a treatment used for neoplastic disease of the vulva when surgical resection is not feasible. It is not utilized in the treatment of condyloma acuminata. Educational Objective: Soft, pink, papillary lesions on the external genitalia are consistent with condyloma acuminata, which are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). The goal of treatment of condyloma acuminata is to destroy the affected cells but many methods can be used to achieve this. Topical formulations of podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid, fluorouracil, or liquid nitrogen are first-line therapy options.

questionStem: A 68-year-old woman has dysuria , nocturia , and frequent urination . Several urine cultures have been negative . Her condition is most likely caused by decreased production of which of the following hormones?
correctExplanation: This postmenopausal patient's symptoms of dysuria, nocturia, and frequent urination are consistent with a diagnosis of genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which is secondary to vulvovaginal atrophy in the setting of decreased estradiol production. Estradiol is crucial for the maintenance of the soft tissue structure, vasculature, and mucous secretions of the vulva and vagina, as well as of the lower urinary tract. Postmenopausal atrophy of these structures leads to increased symptoms of dryness and pruritus, as well as urinary symptoms of dysuria, urinary frequency, and hematuria, and an increased risk for urinary tract infections. The genital and urinary symptoms of vulvovaginal atrophy respond to topical estradiol cream.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Androstenedione (Choice A) is the precursor to testosterone (Choice E). Both hormones may be converted to estradiol via aromatase. While serum concentrations of both androstenedione and testosterone are decreased in postmenopausal women, this is not responsible for genitourinary atrophy, which is directly mediated by estradiol. Progesterone (Choice C) is a sex hormone that is important during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. It may be prescribed to postmenopausal women in combination with estrogen in order to treat symptoms of menopause without increasing the risk for endometrial carcinoma, which is increased in postmenopausal women who have not undergone hysterectomy and who are treated with estradiol alone. The pathogenesis of vulvovaginal atrophy is not mediated by progesterone. Prostaglandins (Choice D) are important in the regulation of the menstrual cycle and labor and may be given as an agent to induce labor. Prostaglandins do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis or treatment of vulvovaginal atrophy. Educational Objective: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause occurs as a sequela of vulvovaginal atrophy because of the decreased production of estradiol. Patients present with symptoms of vaginal dryness and pruritus, as well as urinary symptoms of dysuria, urinary frequency, and hematuria, and an increased risk for urinary tract infections. Treatment is with topical estradiol cream.

questionStem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 27 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 5 hours after the sudden onset of increasingly severe abdominal pain and a 3-hour history of nausea , vomiting , chills , and worsening malaise . She reports good fetal movement. She has had mild uterine contractions . She has not had vaginal bleeding or loss of vaginal fluid. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness to palpation with exquisite tenderness in the right lower quadrant ; there is no guarding or rebound . On pelvic examination , the cervix is nulliparous and closed . She is unable to tolerate a bimanual examination because of extreme tenderness . Her leukocyte count is 16,700/mm 3• External fetal monitoring shows a heart rate of 170/min with moderate variability . There are spontaneous accelerations and no decelerations . An external tocometer shows intermittent uterine contractions . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Appendicitis classically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. McBurney point, a sensitive location for tenderness on palpation, is located at two-thirds the distance between the umbilicus and the inguinal ligament, because this is the common position of the appendix. In pregnancy, as a result of the location of the enlarging uterus, the appendix may be displaced superiorly as compared to that of a nongravid patient. This displacement limits the classic history and physical examination, which rely on a right lower quadrant position of the appendix. When displaced cephalad, parietal peritoneal inflammation may no longer occur at the McBurney point, even migrating as cephalad as the right upper quadrant, mimicking diagnoses such as cholecystitis. Diagnosis is facilitated by CT scans (though less ideal in pregnancy because of the risk for teratogenicity to the fetus), MRI, or ultrasonography, which may show appendiceal enlargement, the presence of an appendicolith, appendiceal wall thickening, or periappendiceal fluid or fat stranding. Fetal heart tracings are usually reassuring unless maternal hemodynamics have been compromised, and fetal tachycardia may result in response to maternal fever. Treatment is with urgent appendectomy to prevent complications such as appendiceal rupture, sepsis, preterm labor, and death.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cholecystitis (Choice B) presents with signs that may mimic some aspects of appendicitis, such as fever, nausea, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. However, cholecystitis typically causes right upper quadrant pain that may be elicited by pressure applied to the right upper quadrant during deep inspiration and leads to termination of the breath (Murphy sign), rather than right lower quadrant pain. It is important to note that cephalad displacement of the appendix by the gravid uterus may cause appendicitis to produce right upper quadrant pain in some patients, mimicking cholecystitis. Chorioamnionitis (Choice C) is a bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in the setting of premature or prolonged rupture of membranes. Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation. Pelvic inflammatory disease (Choice D) is inflammation of the uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, and usually occurs secondary to infection with the sexually transmitted organisms Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Peritonitis may ensue in advanced cases. The absence of abnormal cervical discharge, cervicitis, or cervical motion tenderness, as well as the presence of exquisite right lower quadrant tenderness render this a less likely diagnosis in this patient. Pyelonephritis (Choice E) typically presents with fevers, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain with associated costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination. This most commonly occurs from ascending urinary tract infections. While pregnant patients are at an increased risk for pyelonephritis, the absence of costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms render this diagnosis less likely than appendicitis. Educational Objective: Acute appendicitis may occur in gravid women and presents with right lower quadrant (or variably right-sided pain based on the location of the appendix) or periumbilical abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. Treatment is with urgent appendectomy.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 39 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor after spontaneous rupture of membranes . The amniotic fluid is clear, and the fetal heart tracing shows a rate of 150/min with no evidence of deceleration . Her first pregnancy ended in vaginal delivery at term, and her second pregnancy ended in cesarean delivery for breech presentation at term. Eight hours later, the cervix is 100% effaced and 10 cm dilated ; the vertex is at O station . The fetal heart rate is now 140/min , but there is a sudden decrease in fetal heart rate variability followed by a prolonged fetal heart rate deceleration to 60-70/min for 3 minutes . The patient develops increasing lower abdominal pain. There is no vaginal bleeding . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Uterine rupture is a dangerous complication of pregnancy wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. Severe pain is a common initial finding. Hemodynamic instability can manifest in the mother with tachycardia and hypotension, and in the fetus with late decelerations, tachycardia, bradycardia, or loss of beat-to-beat variability. If uterine rupture occurs during labor, sudden loss of fetal station is a highly suggestive finding. Fetal parts may be palpable above the fundus with Leopold maneuvers. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after cesarean delivery, multiparity, and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. Uterine rupture is treated with emergent laparotomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) is a premature separation of the placenta from the uterine endometrium. Presenting findings include abdominal or pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, and tetanic contractions. An abnormal fetal heart rate may be detected, and fetal demise may occur if the abruption is large. The patient's acute onset of symptoms during labor and her history of prior cesarean delivery are more concerning for uterine rupture. Maternal supine position (Choice B) may lead to aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus, which may result in maternal hypotension, syncope, tachycardia, pallor, and diaphoresis. If severe, maternal hypotension may lead to placental hypoperfusion and fetal distress. The abrupt onset of pain during delivery with a sudden change in fetal hemodynamics is more consistent with uterine rupture than with aortocaval compression. Umbilical cord compression (Choice C) is an intrapartum complication wherein the fetal umbilical cord becomes compressed and impairs fetal oxygenation, which may be immediately life threatening. Fetal bradycardia and late decelerations are common presenting findings. Causes of umbilical cord compression include oligohydramnios, cord prolapse, nuchal cord, or a cord that is tangled or knotted. The mother would not experience increasing abdominal pain because of umbilical cord compression. Variable fetal heart rate deceleration (Choice E) is often caused by umbilical cord compression. Variable decelerations are rapid, abrupt, and non-sustained, and are characterized by a decrease in fetal heart rate of greater than 15/min, an implicit time from onset of deceleration to its nadir of less than 30 seconds, and duration between 15 seconds and 2 minutes. Educational Objective: Uterine rupture is a dangerous obstetric complication where the uterine wall tears. Acute pain and both maternal and fetal hemodynamic instability, along with the sudden loss of fetal station are suggestive findings. Treatment is with emergent laparotomy.

questionStem: During a routine health maintenance examination , a 54-year-old woman is found to have a 2-cm left axillary lymph node. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Laboratory studies , an x-ray of the chest, and mammography show normal findings . A biopsy specimen of the node shows adenocarcinoma . Which of the following is the most likely site of the primary cancer?
correctExplanation: In patients with axillary lymphadenopathy that demonstrates adenocarcinoma on biopsy, breast cancer should be suspected. Breast cancer, the most common non-dermatologic malignancy in women, typically consists of two main histologic subtypes, ductal or lobular adenocarcinoma, and can present with a breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy caused by an underlying occult breast cancer, as in this patient. In patients with axillary lymphadenopathy, mammography should be the first diagnostic step. If negative for an underlying mass, a biopsy of the palpable lymph node should be obtained. As well, MRI of the breast should be considered following a negative mammogram, as it is more sensitive and specific for breast lesions. This patient's chest x-ray did not demonstrate lymphadenopathy in other locations, which is reassuring that this patient may have curable stage 11, or early-stage, breast cancer. In patients with early-stage breast cancer, treatment consists of surgical removal of the tumor and axillary lymph nodes along with adjuvant systemic hormonal therapy, biologic therapy, or chemotherapy, which depends on the estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptor positivity of the cancer. Patients with advanced breast cancer are typically treated with life­ prolonging, palliative systemic therapy only.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Lung adenocarcinoma (Choice B), pancreatic adenocarcinoma (Choice D), and stomach adenocarcinoma (Choice E) are unlikely to metastasize to the axillary lymph nodes only. Lung adenocarcinoma may initially metastasize to the mediastinal, hilar, or bronchial lymph nodes. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma typically metastasizes to the peripancreatic and para-aortic lymph nodes initially. Stomach adenocarcinoma may spread to local perigastric lymph nodes, along with the Sister Mary Joseph lymph node in the umbilical region or the Virchow lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Cancer of the lymphatic system (Choice C) typically presents as lymphoma, a proliferation of neoplastic monoclonal lymphocytes. Primary adenocarcinoma of the lymphatic system is not known to occur. Educational Objective: Breast cancer typically consists of ductal or lobular adenocarcinoma. It can present with a breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy as a result of an underlying occult breast cancer. In patients with axillary lymphadenopathy, physicians should investigate for breast cancer using mammography. If the mammography shows no abnormalities, biopsy of the palpable lymph node and MRI of the breast should be obtained next.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. She had a fracture of the right femur 12 months ago that required open reduction and a blood transfusion . Her current partner is the father of all her children . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation . Her blood group is 0 , Rh-negative . Indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for anti-Kell antibody at a titer of 1 :256. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: 24-Hour urine collection for measurement of protein and creatinine clearance
choices.B: Kell tyl'.)ing of the father's blood
choices.D: Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid

correctExplanation: A mother can develop antibodies against red blood cell (RBC) antigens after being exposed to fetal blood antigens during delivery or from a previous blood transfusion. In this case, this patient likely developed antibodies to the Kell RBC antigen after being exposed to it in her blood transfusion. Because maternal antibodies can cross the placenta, it is important to determine whether this patient's fetus has Kell-positive or Kell-negative RBCs. If her fetus had Kell-positive RBCs, the antibodies created by her immune system would cause hemolysis of the fetal erythrocytes, leading to severe fetal hemolytic anemia (eg, erythroblastosis fetalis) and likely fetal demise. As the mother has no signs of hemolysis in the presence of anti-Kell antibodies, her RBCs do not have Kell antigens and she would not have contributed a Kell antigen to her fetus. The easiest way to determine the antigen status of the fetus is to determine the antigen status of the father. If he is Kell-negative as well, then the fetus will be Kell-negative and there is no risk for erythroblastosis fetalis. However, if he is positive, there is a possibility that their child will be Kell antigen-positive and suffer from erythroblastosis fetalis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. 24-Hour urine collection for measurement of protein and creatinine clearance (Choice A) is used to diagnose preeclampsia in the setting of hypertension. However, this patient is at only 8 weeks of gestation, whereas preeclampsia typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. Liver function tests (Choice C) would demonstrate abnormalities in transaminases or bilirubin and may be useful in the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets). It also typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid (Choice D) can be used to determine whether the fetus is experiencing hemolysis. However, sampling would be unnecessary if Kell typing of the father disclosed that he was Kell-negative, making this an inappropriate initial action. Intravenous lgG therapy (Choice E) can be used to treat autoimmune diseases and could have possibly prevented the development of Kell antibodies if it had been given at the time of blood transfusion. However, it plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis in the setting of active anti-Kell antibodies. Intravenous Rh0(D) immune globulin therapy (Choice F) is used to prevent alloimmunization to the Rh(D) antigen in Rh(D)-negative women when they are potentially exposed to fetal blood. It plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis because of anti-Kell antibodies. Educational Objective: Antigens on the fetal RBCs depend on the antigens of each parent's RBCs. If the mother exhibits antibodies against a specific RBC antigen, whether from a previous pregnancy or a blood transfusion, the fetus is at risk for erythroblastosis fetalis if it carries that antigen, as maternal lgG antibodies can cross the placenta. The first step in determining the potential RBC antigens of a fetus is to determine the antigen type of each parent.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period . She is 150 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m 2• Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. The cervix is visualized , and the vaginal mucosa is hypoestrogenized . Serum studies show a luteinizing hormone concentration of 22 mlU/mL , follicle-stimulating hormone concentration of 33 mlU/mL , and prolactin concentration of 9 ng/ml. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Turner syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is secondary to gonadal (ovarian) dysgenesis in the setting of a 45,XO genotype. Other signs of Turner syndrome include a short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. Additionally, as a result of decreased estrogen concentrations, patients fail to develop mature secondary sexual characteristics of breast and pubic hair development. As well, patients may develop vaginal atrophy or dryness related to low estrogen concentrations, like postmenopausal patients. Vital signs will be within normal limits, and diagnosis is made through a karyotype analysis. Other labs that may aid in diagnosis are increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle­ stimulating hormone (FSH) as a result of the lack of negative feedback from estrogen, but these findings are nonspecific.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) presents with extremely low body weight, fear of weight gain, and dysphoria, as well as bradycardia and lanugo on physical examination. While it can present with amenorrhea as a result of suppression of the hypothalamic-ovarian-pituitary axis, it is unlikely in this patient with an overweight BMI. Congenital absence of the uterus (Choice B) is because of an error in the normal development of the Mullerian system that results in complete absence of the uterus and, occasionally, the upper vagina. However, these patients will have functional ovaries and therefore adequate maturation of secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast and pubic hair development. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice D) presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, most commonly to the result of a pituitary gland adenoma. High concentrations of prolactin inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone and subsequently cause decreased concentrations of FSH and LH. This patient's prolactin concentration is within reference ranges. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Choice E) leads to amenorrhea as caused by the decreased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, which results in impaired follicle maturation and ovulation, as well as a lack of development of secondary sexual characteristics. This patient's FSH and LH are within reference ranges, making this an unlikely diagnosis. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Choice F) most commonly presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses because of anovulation secondary to increased androgen concentrations. The LH to FSH ratio is typically increased, and ultrasonography of the pelvis will show numerous ovarian follicular cysts. It is more commonly associated with secondary oligomenorrhea than primary amenorrhea. Pregnancy (Choice G) causes amenorrhea as the endometrial lining is maintained to support the developing embryo. However, it typically causes secondary amenorrhea in a sexually active patient, rather than primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is because of ovarian dysgenesis. Other signs include the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. LH and FSH concentrations are typically increased because of the absence of negative feedback from estrogen, and diagnosis is made with a karyotype analysis.

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 14 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. She has a history of multiple sexually transmitted diseases . Her last tetanus toxoid injection was 5 years ago. Her 4-year-old daughter developed a low-grade fever, respiratory symptoms , and a rash 24 hours ago. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 14-week gestation . Fetal heart tones are heard . Hepatitis B surface antigen assay is negative , and rubella titer is less than 1 :8. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccination for this patient?
correctExplanation: Maternal immunization is important for both maternal and fetal health. Ideally, vaccinations are given prior to conception, but some vaccinations are safe to administer during pregnancy. Live attenuated vaccines are made of viable viral pathogens whose virulence has been reduced. However, if a mutation were to occur in the viral genome to revert the attenuation, the infection could be contracted. Live attenuated vaccines include those to measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), yellow fever, intranasal influenza, smallpox, varicella-zoster, rotavirus, and the oral poliovirus vaccines. As a rule, live vaccinations should be avoided during pregnancy because of the risk, although low, of contracting the disease. In contrast, inactivated vaccines are made by killing the virus, which makes it safe to administer to pregnant patients. Vaccinations considered to be safe in pregnancy that are routinely given to all pregnant patients include the tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) and influenza vaccines. Additional vaccinations may be warranted depending on the patient's immunization status and degree of risk for contracting preventable infections. In this case, the patient is not immunized against hepatitis B or rubella infection. The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant vaccine with no known potential for causing harm in the mother or fetus and is safe to administer during pregnancy. However, as the rubella vaccine is part of the MMR live attenuated vaccine, it is not administered during pregnancy. The patient will likely also need a Tdap vaccine later in her pregnancy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Inactivated poliovirus (Choice B), or the Salk poliovirus vaccine, is not necessary in this patient as there is no indication that she was not previously immunized to poliovirus, as is standard. The Sabin poliovirus is an oral, live attenuated virus, which would be contraindicated during pregnancy. Measles (Choice C), mumps (Choice D), and rubella (Choice E) are given together in the MMR vaccine. This is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. However, this vaccine should be administered to the patient following her pregnancy. Tetanus vaccination is recommended during pregnancy but with the Tdap vaccine, not the tetanus toxoid (Choice E) vaccine. The Tdap vaccine also immunizes against Bordetella pertussis, the causative pathogen of whooping cough. This allows maternal antibodies to develop and cross the placenta, providing some protection to the fetus and infant until they can receive their own pertussis vaccination at the age of 2 months. Administration of the Tdap vaccine to all pregnant women is an important preventative strategy against pertussis. Educational Objective: Maternal immunization is important for both maternal and fetal health. Live attenuated vaccines, such as MMR, should be avoided during pregnancy and given following pregnancy, if necessary. Tdap and inactivated influenza vaccines are given routinely to all pregnant patients and additional immunizations, including hepatitis B, may be given on a case-by-case basis.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of heavy vaginal bleeding for the past 3 days. She has no history of serious illness. Menopause occurred 6 years ago. A Pap smear 1 year ago showed no abnormalities . Physical examination today shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows an irregularly shaped uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dl , and hematocrit is 27%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration
choices.C: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens), iatrogenic, or idiopathic. In postmenopausal patients and patients over the age of 45, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The most appropriate next step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. A hysteroscopy with sampling allows for a more complete evaluation of the endometrium (eg, polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentration (Choice A) would not disclose the cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in this patient. FSH is increased in postmenopausal patients but is not useful in the evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. In endometrial carcinoma, the measurement of cancer antigen 125 can be used for the surveillance of patients' disease progression. MRI of the pelvis (Choice B) may be used to evaluate myometrial, cervical, or lymph node invasion and metastasis of endometrial carcinoma but is infrequently used. MRI would not be the next step in the evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, which is more definitively evaluated by tissue sampling. Transfusion of packed red blood cells (Choice C) is generally not necessary in a stable patient with a hemoglobin concentration greater than 7 g/dl. The patient in the question has a hemoglobin of 9 g/dl and does not meet criteria to receive a transfusion at this time. Hysterectomy (Choice E) may be indicated if endometrial carcinoma is diagnosed. However, in a patient with abnormal uterine bleeding, prior steps need to be taken to diagnose the cause of the abnormal uterine bleeding. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding refers to irregular menstrual bleeding that may be abnormal in quality, duration, or timing.
